Lecture 22

Nesting and the Hubbard model

What this lecture does

Every model since Lecture 15 has had one set of rapidities. Give the particles a spin and that stops being enough: the two-body S-matrix becomes a matrix on the labels, and carrying a particle round the ring acts on a vector instead of multiplying by a number. The quantisation condition is then an eigenvalue problem, and this lecture’s one idea is that the eigenvalue problem is itself an integrable model — an inhomogeneous Heisenberg chain whose sites are the gas’s own particles — solved by the algebraic Bethe ansatz of Lecture 18. That brings a second set of rapidities and a second layer of Bethe equations. Then the Hubbard model, whose equations have the same shape with kkk replaced by sin⁡k\sin ksink.

22.1 Fermions with a spin, and a matrix S-matrix

The model is Lecture 16’s delta gas with one addition: each particle carries a spin-12\tfrac1221​ label, and the particles are fermions. On a ring of circumference LLL, H=−∑j=1N∂2∂xj2+2c∑i<jδ(xi−xj),c>0, H=-\sum_{j=1}^{N}\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial x_j^{2}} +2c\sum_{i<j}\delta(x_i-x_j),\qquad c>0, H=−j=1∑N​∂xj2​∂2​+2ci<j∑​δ(xi​−xj​),c>0,(22.1) acting on wavefunctions ψ(x1σ1,…,xNσN)\psi(x_1\sigma_1,\dots,x_N\sigma_N)ψ(x1​σ1​,…,xN​σN​), σj∈{↑,↓}\sigma_j\in\{\uparrow,\downarrow\}σj​∈{↑,↓}, that are totally antisymmetric under exchanging a position and its label together. This is the Yang–Gaudin model (Yang 1967, Gaudin 1967). Write MMM for the number of down spins, so Sz=N2−MS^{z}=\tfrac N2-MSz=2N​−M, and take M≤N/2M\le N/2M≤N/2.

Units are Lecture 16’s, ℏ=2m=1\hbar=2m=1ℏ=2m=1, kinetic operator −∑∂j2-\sum\partial_j^{2}−∑∂j2​ — not the ℏ=m=1\hbar=m=1ℏ=m=1 of Lecture 21 (Remark 21.1). The two-body problem is two problems

Lecture 16 did the two-body problem for labelled particles. On x1<x2x_1<x_2x1​<x2​ write ψ(x1,x2)=A ei(k1x1+k2x2)+A′ ei(k2x1+k1x2),A,A′∈C2⊗C2, \psi(x_1,x_2)=A\,e^{\ii(k_1x_1+k_2x_2)}+A'\,e^{\ii(k_2x_1+k_1x_2)}, \qquad A,A'\in\C^{2}\otimes\C^{2}, ψ(x1​,x2​)=Aei(k1​x1​+k2​x2​)+A′ei(k2​x1​+k1​x2​),A,A′∈C2⊗C2,(22.2) with slot jjj of the tensor holding the label of the particle at position jjj, and extend by antisymmetry. Proposition 16.6 gives A′=YF(k1−k2)AA'=Y_{\mathrm F}(k_1-k_2)AA′=YF​(k1​−k2​)A with YF(k)=−kP+ick+ic=S(k) Π−−Π+,S(k)=k−ick+ic, Y_{\mathrm F}(k)=-\frac{k\perm+\ii c}{k+\ii c} =S(k)\,\Pi_--\Pi_+,\qquad S(k)=\frac{k-\ii c}{k+\ii c}, YF​(k)=−k+ickP+ic​=S(k)Π−​−Π+​,S(k)=k+ick−ic​,(22.3) P\permP the permutation of the two label factors (Definition 8.3) and Π±=12(1±P)\Pi_\pm=\tfrac12(\Id\pm\perm)Π±​=21​(1±P) the projectors on labels symmetric and antisymmetric checked.

(22.3) is the whole reason this lecture exists. On the singlet — labels antisymmetric, positions symmetric — the delta acts and the amplitude picks up Lecture 16’s scalar S(k)S(k)S(k). On the triplet the wavefunction vanishes where the particles meet, the delta never sees them, and the amplitude picks up −1-1−1 (Figure 22.1). One two-body problem, two answers; a scalar Bethe equation cannot hold both.

The product of crossings is a transfer matrix

(22.9) is NNN eigenvalue problems for NNN different operators, which looks hopeless. It is not: the NNN operators are values of one commuting family, and it is a family we have already solved.

Definition 22.3 (The auxiliary chain). Put ξj=kj/c\xi_j=k_j/cξj​=kj​/c, adjoin an auxiliary C2\C^{2}C2 labelled aaa, and set Ta(λ)=XaN(λ−ξN)⋯Xa1(λ−ξ1),t(λ)=tra⁡Ta(λ). T_a(\bethe)=X_{aN}(\bethe-\xi_N)\cdots X_{a1}(\bethe-\xi_1), \qquad \transfer(\bethe)=\tra T_a(\bethe). Ta​(λ)=XaN​(λ−ξN​)⋯Xa1​(λ−ξ1​),t(λ)=tra​Ta​(λ).(22.13)

Its quantum spaces are the labels of the particles and its NNN “sites” are the particles themselves, at inhomogeneities ξj\xi_jξj​ equal to their own momenta in units of the coupling. There is no lattice and no spin Hamiltonian: the chain is a bookkeeping device that happens to be an integrable model.

Proposition 22.5 (The chain is Heisenberg). Ta(λ)=(−1)N[∏n(λ−ξn+i)]−1 LaN(λ−ξN)⋯La1(λ−ξ1)T_a(\bethe)=(-1)^{N}\big[\prod_n(\bethe-\xi_n+\ii)\big]^{-1}\, \Lop{aN}(\bethe-\xi_N)\cdots\Lop{a1}(\bethe-\xi_1)Ta​(λ)=(−1)N[∏n​(λ−ξn​+i)]−1LaN​(λ−ξN​)⋯La1​(λ−ξ1​): the auxiliary chain is the inhomogeneous Heisenberg chain of Lecture 18’s reading, up to one scalar. Proof. The displayed identity is (22.4) factor by factor. The RTTRTTRTT relation (Theorem 17.3) needs only that every site operator obeys RLLR\Lop{}\Lop{}RL​L​ with one common R\RmatR, and the shifts cancel in the argument of R\RmatR, (λ−ξn)−(μ−ξn)=λ−μ(\bethe-\xi_n)-(\mu-\xi_n)=\bethe-\mu(λ−ξn​)−(μ−ξn​)=λ−μ, so commutativity follows as in Lecture 17; scalars commute with everything checked. 

So all NNN conditions can be imposed at once: ask for a common eigenvector of the family t(λ)\transfer(\bethe)t(λ) and read off the NNN numbers t(ξa)\transfer(\xi_a)t(ξa​). This is the whole of nesting. The first Bethe ansatz reduced the gas to a finite linear-algebra problem in the labels; the second solves that problem.

22.3 The nested Bethe equations

Lecture 18 solved this chain. Two features deserve to be said aloud.

The two sets do different jobs. The kjk_jkj​ are momenta and carry the energy (22.18). The counting. At zero total momentum the same root comes out of a problem with no Bethe ansatz in it at all — a delta well on a circle — which the tutorial does checked.

Whether these solutions exhaust the spectrum is a separate question, and the answer is §15.6’s: they do not, without the complex ones. The reading at the end says what is known cited: Takahashi ch. 12; Essler et al. ch. 4.

22.4 The Hubbard model

What is proved in this section, and what is not. The Hubbard model’s Bethe equations are stated; their derivation, which is a nested algebraic Bethe ansatz over an R\RmatR-matrix that this course has not built, is cited. What is done here: the two-body problem is solved on the lattice, in the tutorial, and it fixes the correspondence with §22.3 including the sign; the equations are then checked against exact diagonalisation of a six-site ring, where 202020 of the 212121 states of the singlet sector are regular Bethe states and the twenty-first is the η\etaη-pair of Remark 22.10. Eighteen of the twenty — those with K≠πK\ne\piK=π, complex roots included — are checked to 10−1410^{-14}10−14 by reconstructing the roots from (K,E)(K,E)(K,E); that reconstruction degenerates at K=πK=\piK=π, so the two states there are checked directly against the equations instead checked. The SO(4)SO(4)SO(4) commutators are computed exactly, on one even ring.

On a ring of LLL sites — LLL even, which Remark 22.10 needs and nothing before it does — with cjσ†c^{\dagger}_{j\sigma}cjσ†​ creating an electron of spin σ\sigmaσ at site jjj and njσ=cjσ†cjσn_{j\sigma}=c^{\dagger}_{j\sigma}c_{j\sigma}njσ​=cjσ†​cjσ​, H=−t∑j=1L∑σ(cjσ†cj+1,σ+cj+1,σ†cjσ)+U∑j=1Lnj↑nj↓. H=-t\sum_{j=1}^{L}\sum_{\sigma} \big(c^{\dagger}_{j\sigma}c_{j+1,\sigma}+c^{\dagger}_{j+1,\sigma}c_{j\sigma}\big) +U\sum_{j=1}^{L}n_{j\uparrow}n_{j\downarrow}. H=−tj=1∑L​σ∑​(cjσ†​cj+1,σ​+cj+1,σ†​cjσ​)+Uj=1∑L​nj↑​nj↓​.(22.21) Only U/tU/tU/t matters, and we set t=1t=1t=1 from here. It is the Yang–Gaudin gas put on a lattice: two species, and an interaction that acts only when they meet. Two things change at once — the dispersion becomes −2cos⁡k-2\cos k−2cosk instead of k2k^{2}k2, and the delta becomes an on-site energy — and that the two conspire into the single substitution (22.24) is a result, not an observation. The dispersion is what makes it hard: −2cos⁡k-2\cos k−2cosk is not a quadratic form, so there is no Galilean invariance and no centre-of-mass separation.

Theorem 22.9 (Lieb and Wu 1968). The regular eigenstates of (22.21) with NNN electrons and MMM down spins — those with finite, pairwise distinct roots, and 2M≤N≤L2M\le N\le L2M≤N≤L — are given by charge momenta k1,…,kNk_1,\dots,k_Nk1​,…,kN​ and spin rapidities Λ1,…,ΛM\Lambda_1,\dots,\Lambda_MΛ1​,…,ΛM​ solving eikjL=∏α=1Msin⁡kj−Λα+iU/4sin⁡kj−Λα−iU/4,∏j=1NΛα−sin⁡kj+iU/4Λα−sin⁡kj−iU/4=∏β≠αΛα−Λβ+iU/2Λα−Λβ−iU/2,\begin{align} e^{\ii k_jL}&=\prod_{\alpha=1}^{M} \frac{\sin k_j-\Lambda_\alpha+\ii U/4}{\sin k_j-\Lambda_\alpha-\ii U/4},\tag{22.22}\\ \prod_{j=1}^{N}\frac{\Lambda_\alpha-\sin k_j+\ii U/4}{\Lambda_\alpha-\sin k_j-\ii U/4} &=\prod_{\beta\ne\alpha}\frac{\Lambda_\alpha-\Lambda_\beta+\ii U/2}{\Lambda_\alpha-\Lambda_\beta-\ii U/2}, \tag{22.23}\end{align}eikj​Lj=1∏N​Λα​−sinkj​−iU/4Λα​−sinkj​+iU/4​​=α=1∏M​sinkj​−Λα​−iU/4sinkj​−Λα​+iU/4​,=β=α∏​Λα​−Λβ​−iU/2Λα​−Λβ​+iU/2​,​(22.22)(22.23)​ with E=−2∑jcos⁡kjE=-2\sum_j\cos k_jE=−2∑j​coskj​ cited: Lieb and Wu (1968); Essler et al. ch. 3. They are not all the states, and not all the rest are symmetry descendants either: at isolated couplings a pair of charge momenta collides and leaves a state that is neither. The reading gives one, on the six-site ring. Completeness is a counting statement with known exceptions and a subject of its own cited: Essler et al. §3.2.6, ch. 4.

Compare (22.22)–(22.23) with (22.16)–(22.17), written in physical units with Λα=cλα\Lambda_\alpha=c\bethe_\alphaΛα​=cλα​: they are the same equations under kj⟼sin⁡kj,c⟼U2t. k_j\longmapsto\sin k_j,\qquad c\longmapsto \frac{U}{2t}. kj​⟼sinkj​,c⟼2tU​.(22.24) The lattice replaces the momentum by its sine, and the coupling by U/2tU/2tU/2t — with that sign. Getting it wrong is not a convention: with c↦−U/2tc\mapsto-U/2tc↦−U/2t not one of the eighteen singlet states of the two-electron L=6L=6L=6 ring satisfies (22.22), and with the right sign all eighteen do checked. Remark 22.10 (SO(4)SO(4)SO(4)). (22.21) has more symmetry than the spin su(2)su(2)su(2). Let η†=∑j(−1)jcj↑†cj↓†\eta^{\dagger}=\sum_j(-1)^{j}c^{\dagger}_{j\uparrow}c^{\dagger}_{j\downarrow}η†=∑j​(−1)jcj↑†​cj↓†​ create a pair on a site, with the staggering. Then [H,η†]=Uη†,[H,S+]=0,[η†,S+]=0,[H,\eta^{\dagger}]=U\eta^{\dagger},\qquad [H,S^{+}]=0,\qquad [\eta^{\dagger},S^{+}]=0,[H,η†]=Uη†,[H,S+]=0,[η†,S+]=0, all three for even LLL: the hopping terms cancel in pairs along the ring, and the closing bond cancels only if (−1)L=1(-1)^{L}=1(−1)L=1. At L=3L=3L=3, U=7U=7U=7 the commutator misses Uη†U\eta^{\dagger}Uη† by 222 checked. So H−U2N^H-\tfrac U2\hat NH−2U​N^ carries a second su(2)su(2)su(2) commuting with the first. As Lie algebras su(2)⊕su(2)≅so(4)su(2)\oplus su(2)\cong so(4)su(2)⊕su(2)≅so(4); the Z2\Z_2Z2​ of the familiar statement (SU(2)×SU(2))/Z2≅SO(4)(SU(2)\times SU(2))/\Z_2\cong SO(4)(SU(2)×SU(2))/Z2​≅SO(4) lives at the group level, and no commutator can see it.

For the printed HHH the η\etaη’s are spectrum-generating, not symmetries: [H,η†]=Uη†[H,\eta^{\dagger}]=U\eta^{\dagger}[H,η†]=Uη† moves the energy rather than fixing it, and it is H−U2N^H-\tfrac U2\hat NH−2U​N^ whose degeneracies SO(4)SO(4)SO(4) organises cited: Yang (1989); Essler et al. ch. 2. The staggering makes η†\eta^{\dagger}η† anticommute with the translation, so it raises the momentum by π\piπ, and η†∣0⟩\eta^{\dagger}\ket0η†∣0⟩ is an exact eigenstate of (22.21) of energy UUU at K=πK=\piK=π checked — and outside Theorem 22.9, because at K=πK=\piK=π every finite Bethe pair has cos⁡k1+cos⁡k2=0\cos k_1+\cos k_2=0cosk1​+cosk2​=0, so E=0E=0E=0, while exact diagonalisation at L=6L=6L=6 returns 0,00,00,0 and UUU.

There is an R\RmatR-matrix behind (22.22)–(22.23) — Shastry’s, which obeys the Yang–Baxter equation but is not of difference form, depending on the two spectral parameters separately cited: Shastry (1986); Essler et al. ch. 12. Every construction in Lecture 17 and Lecture 18 used the difference property. So the Hubbard model is solvable by these methods and is not an instance of them, which is the honest place to leave it in a one-term course; the reading at the end says what Shastry’s matrix is, and what it is not the reason for. Lecture 23 takes the nested equations (22.16)–(22.17) and (22.22)–(22.23) as given and asks what a gas described by two coupled families of rapidities does out of equilibrium.

22.5 Higher rank: where the Dynkin diagram comes in

Nothing in §22.2 used that the label space is C2\C^{2}C2. For κ\kappaκ species the two-body matrix is still X(u)=R(−u)/(u+i)X(u)=\Rmat(-u)/(u+\ii)X(u)=R(−u)/(u+i) with R(u)=u−iP\Rmat(u)=u-\ii\permR(u)=u−iP on Cκ⊗Cκ\C^{\kappa}\otimes\C^{\kappa}Cκ⊗Cκ, it still obeys the Yang–Baxter equation checked, and Theorem 22.2 and Proposition 22.4 go through word for word. What changes is §22.3. The auxiliary monodromy is now κ×κ\kappa\times\kappaκ×κ in the auxiliary index — the transfer matrix t=tra⁡Ta\transfer=\tra T_at=tra​Ta​ still acts on the κN\kappa^{N}κN-dimensional label space — its reference state breaks slκsl_\kappaslκ​ to slκ−1sl_{\kappa-1}slκ−1​, and its first row carries κ−1\kappa-1κ−1 creation operators B2(λ),…,Bκ(λ)B_2(\bethe),\dots,B_\kappa(\bethe)B2​(λ),…,Bκ​(λ) in place of Lecture 18’s single BBB. A Bethe vector Bi1(λ1)⋯BiM(λM)∣0⟩B_{i_1}(\bethe_1)\cdots B_{i_M}(\bethe_M)\ket0Bi1​​(λ1​)⋯BiM​​(λM​)∣0⟩ therefore carries a vector of indices, and choosing that vector is itself a Bethe-ansatz problem of rank κ−1\kappa-1κ−1, whose auxiliary problem needs another, and so on — κ−1\kappa-1κ−1 levels, the last of them scalar. That is why the procedure is called nesting, and the extra creation operators are what Lecture 18 pointed at.

The bookkeeping is the Lie algebra’s. R(u)=u−iP\Rmat(u)=u-\ii\permR(u)=u−iP commutes with A⊗1+1⊗AA\otimes\Id+\Id\otimes AA⊗1+1⊗A for every A∈slκA\in sl_\kappaA∈slκ​ checked, so the hierarchy is slκsl_\kappaslκ​-invariant, and the κ−1\kappa-1κ−1 levels are the nodes of the Dynkin diagram Aκ−1A_{\kappa-1}Aκ−1​: level aaa carries MaM_aMa​ rapidities λ(a)\bethe^{(a)}λ(a), and the equations couple level aaa to level bbb through the Cartan matrix, ∏j=1Nλα(a)−ξj+i2δa1λα(a)−ξj−i2δa1=∏b=1κ−1 ∏β(b,β)≠(a,α)λα(a)−λβ(b)+iCab/2λα(a)−λβ(b)−iCab/2,C=(2−1−12) for A2, \prod_{j=1}^{N} \frac{\bethe^{(a)}_\alpha-\xi_j+\tfrac\ii2\delta_{a1}} {\bethe^{(a)}_\alpha-\xi_j-\tfrac\ii2\delta_{a1}} =\prod_{b=1}^{\kappa-1}\ \prod_{\substack{\beta\\(b,\beta)\ne(a,\alpha)}} \frac{\bethe^{(a)}_\alpha-\bethe^{(b)}_\beta+\ii C_{ab}/2} {\bethe^{(a)}_\alpha-\bethe^{(b)}_\beta-\ii C_{ab}/2}, \qquad C=\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\-1&2\end{pmatrix}\ \text{for }A_2, j=1∏N​λα(a)​−ξj​−2i​δa1​λα(a)​−ξj​+2i​δa1​​=b=1∏κ−1​ β(b,β)=(a,α)​∏​λα(a)​−λβ(b)​−iCab​/2λα(a)​−λβ(b)​+iCab​/2​,C=(2−1​−12​) for A2​,(22.25) the source appearing only at the node the particles attach to — the left-hand side is 111 at every other node, δa1=0\delta_{a1}=0δa1​=0 — and the term (b,β)=(a,α)(b,\beta)=(a,\alpha)(b,β)=(a,α) excluded: with Caa=2C_{aa}=2Caa​=2 it would contribute i/(−i)=−1\ii/(-\ii)=-1i/(−i)=−1 and turn the κ=2\kappa=2κ=2 case into 1=−11=-11=−1 checked. Equation (22.17) is that κ=2\kappa=2κ=2 case (Figure 22.5); the A2A_2A2​ pair, whose second equation contains no ξ\xiξ at all, is in the reading cited: Sutherland (1968), (16)–(17); Babelon, de Vega and Viallet (1982).

The same diagram indexes the other series once the label space carries a different representation, and then the representation data — weights, matrix elements of the generators — is what the computation needs; the rep-engine package supplies it exactly, and the check script takes sl3sl_3sl3​’s fundamental from it.

This is where Lecture 12’s reading returns: there the root systems AN−1A_{N-1}AN−1​, BNB_NBN​, CNC_NCN​, DND_NDN​ indexed classical Calogero–Moser models, one interaction per positive root; here Aκ−1A_{\kappa-1}Aκ−1​ indexes the levels of a quantum Bethe ansatz, one set of rapidities per node. The same combinatorial object, two unrelated uses, and no theorem in this course connecting them.

The root system of slNsl_NslN​, indexing the classical Calogero–Moser models — one pair interaction per positive root (Lecture 12, reading) ⟶\longrightarrow⟶ the Dynkin diagram of Aκ−1A_{\kappa-1}Aκ−1​, indexing the levels of the nested Bethe ansatz for κ\kappaκ-component particles — one set of rapidities per node, coupled by the Cartan matrix (22.25) (type A, cited)

Elastic non-diffractive scattering: no new asymptotic momenta appear, the set is only permuted, and what a collision leaves behind is a displacement (Lecture 9, export E6; the separation itself is Theorem 9.9, cited) ⟶\longrightarrow⟶ the momenta are still only permuted (Equation (22.18)) and the collision still leaves a phase, but the labels are transported by XXX (Figure 22.2), so the ring condition is an eigenvalue problem and not a number (type A; the Part II side proved, the Part I side cited)

22.6 Shastry’s R-matrix, and two transcription traps

The R-matrix. Shastry (1986) built a two-dimensional vertex model whose transfer matrix commutes with (22.21), by taking two six-vertex models at their free-fermion point and coupling them with a local diagonal factor exp⁡(hC↑C↓/2)\exp(hC^{\uparrow}C^{\downarrow}/2)exp(hC↑C↓/2) whose parameter is tied to the spectral one by sinh⁡2h=usin⁡2z\sinh2h=u\sin2zsinh2h=usin2z. Two things are worth separating. Jordan–Wigner is the transformation between the fermions and the spin variables, not the coupling. And the loss of difference form is not what stops t\transfert at a special point from being the shift operator: that is regularity, R(z,z)∝P\Rmat(z,z)\propto\permR(z,z)∝P, which Shastry’s matrix has. What difference form buys is one R\RmatR generating a whole commuting family from a single argument, which is what Lecture 17’s construction used cited: Shastry (1986); Essler et al. ch. 12.

The other nodes. For A2A_2A2​ the second node of (22.25) reads 1=∏β≠αλα(2)−λβ(2)+iλα(2)−λβ(2)−i∏γλα(2)−λγ(1)−i2λα(2)−λγ(1)+i2,1=\prod_{\beta\ne\alpha} \frac{\bethe^{(2)}_\alpha-\bethe^{(2)}_\beta+\ii} {\bethe^{(2)}_\alpha-\bethe^{(2)}_\beta-\ii} \prod_{\gamma} \frac{\bethe^{(2)}_\alpha-\bethe^{(1)}_\gamma-\tfrac\ii2} {\bethe^{(2)}_\alpha-\bethe^{(1)}_\gamma+\tfrac\ii2},1=β=α∏​λα(2)​−λβ(2)​−iλα(2)​−λβ(2)​+i​γ∏​λα(2)​−λγ(1)​+2i​λα(2)​−λγ(1)​−2i​​, with no ξ\xiξ in it at all: the second level sees the particles only through the first. Sutherland’s original writes both levels with an external minus and the self-root included, which is the same equation once the self-factor −1-1−1 is taken across cited: Sutherland (1968), (16)–(17).

The two statistics. The bosonic XB=R(u)/(u+i)X_{\mathrm B}=\Rmat(u)/(u+\ii)XB​=R(u)/(u+i) of Lecture 16 also has XB(0)=−PX_{\mathrm B}(0)=-\permXB​(0)=−P, because R(0)=−iP\Rmat(0)=-\ii\permR(0)=−iP: the two statistics are told apart by u→−uu\to-uu→−u, not by the value at the origin, and Proposition 22.4 holds for both. What they do not share is the periodicity condition checked.

An exceptional state. Theorem 22.9 is restricted to regular solutions, and its escape clause is not decorative. At L=6L=6L=6, N=2N=2N=2, U=23/3U=2\sqrt3/3U=23​/3 the symmetric wavefunction eik0(x+y)(3−∣x−y∣)e^{\ii k_0(x+y)}(3-\abs{x-y})eik0​(x+y)(3−∣x−y∣) with k0=7π/6k_0=7\pi/6k0​=7π/6 is an exact eigenstate of energy 232\sqrt323​ at K=π/3K=\pi/3K=π/3. Any two-root representation of it must satisfy E=−4cos⁡(K/2)cos⁡12(k1−k2)E=-4\cos(K/2)\cos\tfrac12(k_1-k_2)E=−4cos(K/2)cos21​(k1​−k2​), which here forces k1=k2k_1=k_2k1​=k2​: at coincident roots the cusp condition gives A′=−AA'=-AA′=−A and the ordinary ansatz vanishes, so this state is a regularised limit of a colliding pair, reached as q→0q\to0q→0 along k=k0±iqk=k_0\pm\ii qk=k0​±iq. Nor is it a descendant: η\etaη annihilates it and the spin generators preserve the total spin checked.

The Hamiltonian. The reference book writes (22.21) in its particle–hole symmetric form, U∑(n↑−12)(n↓−12)U\sum(n_\uparrow-\tfrac12)(n_\downarrow-\tfrac12)U∑(n↑​−21​)(n↓​−21​), so its energy carries an extra U4(L−2N)\tfrac U4(L-2N)4U​(L−2N); its coupling is u=U/4tu=U/4tu=U/4t, ours is written out; and its spin equation is the reciprocal of (22.23). All three differences are invisible in a formula copied out of context checked.

The gap. §22.7’s Δμ\Delta_\muΔμ​ is the chemical-potential discontinuity. The same book’s Δ\DeltaΔ is the single-holon threshold, exactly half of it, and is printed in Bessel form with u=U/4tu=U/4tu=U/4t. Which gap is meant is not a detail: the two differ by a factor of two at every coupling checked.

22.7 Half filling, the Mott gap, and spin–charge separation

At half filling, N=LN=LN=L, the Hubbard model is an insulator for every U>0U>0U>0. Lieb and Wu’s own paper established it from (22.22)–(22.23) in the thermodynamic limit: the charge gap, meaning the discontinuity μ+−μ−\mu_+-\mu_-μ+​−μ−​ of the chemical potential, is Δμ=16t2U∫1∞y2−1sinh⁡(2πty/U) dy,\Delta_\mu=\frac{16t^{2}}{U}\int_1^{\infty} \frac{\sqrt{y^{2}-1}}{\sinh(2\pi ty/U)}\,\dd y ,Δμ​=U16t2​∫1∞​sinh(2πty/U)y2−1​​dy, positive for every U>0U>0U>0, tending to U−4tU-4tU−4t from above and to (8/π)Ut e−2πt/U(8/\pi)\sqrt{Ut}\,e^{-2\pi t/U}(8/π)Ut​e−2πt/U as U→0U\to0U→0 cited: Lieb and Wu (1968), (21)–(23). Say which gap. The reference book’s Δ\DeltaΔ (its (7.18)) is the single-holon threshold, exactly half of this, and is written in Bessel form with u=U/4tu=U/4tu=U/4t; the two agree to every digit once converted checked. There is no metal–insulator transition at finite UUU in one dimension; the transition is at U=0+U=0^{+}U=0+. The spin sector meanwhile stays gapless, and at large UUU the half-filled model reduces to the Heisenberg antiferromagnet of Lecture 15 with J=4t2/UJ=4t^{2}/UJ=4t2/U: second-order hopping of an electron onto an occupied site and back costs UUU and gains t2t^{2}t2, and it can only happen if the two spins are antiparallel. On a four-site ring, where the Heisenberg ground energy is −3J=−12/U-3J=-12/U−3J=−12/U, the two agree to 0.62%0.62\%0.62% at U=40U=40U=40 and 0.039%0.039\%0.039% at U=160U=160U=160 checked.

That is spin–charge separation, and it is visible already in §22.3: the energy (22.18) does not contain λα\bethe_\alphaλα​. In the thermodynamic limit the two sectors acquire different sound velocities — vcv_{\mathrm c}vc​ from the kkk’s and vsv_{\mathrm s}vs​ from the λ\betheλ’s — and an added electron’s charge and spin propagate apart. The Luttinger-liquid description of the resulting low-energy theory, and the angle-resolved photoemission experiments on quasi-one-dimensional conductors that look for the two dispersing features, are the obvious continuation cited: Essler et al. ch. 8; Giamarchi, Quantum Physics in One Dimension.

Reading

22.8 What is not claimed about the gas

That the solutions of (22.16)–(22.17) exhaust the spectrum is not proved here, and the situation is the one §15.6 described for the Heisenberg chain: real roots do not suffice. Here the complex ones live in the spin sector — strings of λ\betheλ’s, one of which is drawn in Figure 22.4 — while for c>0c>0c>0 the momenta kjk_jkj​ stay real. Proposition 16.4 proves that for the spinless gas; for the spinful one it is Yang’s and Gaudin’s statement, and it is not proved here. Completeness is a counting statement with known exceptions cited: Takahashi ch. 12; Essler et al. ch. 4. The thermodynamics built on that string hypothesis — the analogue of Lecture 20 for two coupled families — is a genuine subject and is not attempted.

Reading

22.9 Bosons with a label, and the attractive gas

Two variants cost one line each and are worth knowing.

Two-component bosons. (22.3) becomes YB=SΠ+−Π−Y_{\mathrm B}=S\Pi_+-\Pi_-YB​=SΠ+​−Π−​, so XB(u)=R(u)/(u+i)X_{\mathrm B}(u)=\Rmat(u)/(u+\ii)XB​(u)=R(u)/(u+i) — the R-matrix itself rather than R(−u)\Rmat(-u)R(−u), and the interacting channel is now the symmetric one. The auxiliary chain is again of Heisenberg type, the fermionic (−1)N−1(-1)^{N-1}(−1)N−1 of (22.9) is absent, and the nested equations come out with the shifts reflected. Substituting the bosonic XXX into the fermionic condition without touching the statistics sign gives eikL=−1e^{\ii kL}=-1eikL=−1 in the singlet: antiperiodic quantisation, and a spectrum wrong by half a level checked.

Attraction. For c<0c<0c<0 the kjk_jkj​ need no longer be real (Proposition 16.4 assumed c>0c>0c>0), and the gas forms bound pairs of one up and one down spin — the one-dimensional analogue of a Cooper pair. In the thermodynamic limit the pair is the string k=cλ±ic/2k=c\bethe\pm\ii c/2k=cλ±ic/2 cited: Gaudin, The Bethe Wavefunction, §11.4, where the string is presented as a large-system approximation. It is not exact on a finite ring: at N=2N=2N=2, K=0K=0K=0, c=−g<0c=-g<0c=−g<0 the even bound wave is cosh⁡q(x−L/2)\cosh q(x-L/2)coshq(x−L/2) with 2qtanh⁡(qL/2)=g2q\tanh(qL/2)=g2qtanh(qL/2)=g, so q>g/2q>g/2q>g/2; at g=1g=1g=1, L=2L=2L=2 the true qqq is 0.77170.77170.7717 against the string’s 0.50.50.5 checked. Nothing in §22.2 used the sign of ccc; everything in §22.3 about real solutions did.

Summary

  • With labels the two-body problem has two answers (22.3): S(k)S(k)S(k) on the singlet, −1-1−1 on the triplet. Following the momenta, a crossing is the matrix X(u)=R(−u)/(u+i)=−L(u)/(u+i)X(u)=\Rmat(-u)/(u+\ii)=-\Lop{}(u)/(u+\ii)X(u)=R(−u)/(u+i)=−L​(u)/(u+i) (22.4), with X(0)=−PX(0)=-\permX(0)=−P, X(u)X(−u)=1X(u)X(-u)=\IdX(u)X(−u)=1 and the Yang–Baxter equation.
  • Periodicity is a matrix condition (Theorem 22.2): (−1)N−1eikaLXaB=B(-1)^{N-1}e^{\ii k_aL}\mathcal X_aB=B(−1)N−1eika​LXa​B=B, with Xa\mathcal X_aXa​ the ordered product of the N−1N-1N−1 crossings particle aaa makes on its way round. The (−1)N−1(-1)^{N-1}(−1)N−1 is the fermionic exchange sign; dropping it replaces the two-body equation by eikL=−(u+i)/(u−i)e^{\ii kL}=-(u+\ii)/(u-\ii)eikL=−(u+i)/(u−i) and doubles the momentum at the sizes checked. The reduction of the N!N!N! conditions to these NNN, on one vector needs the Yang–Baxter equation twice, and its factor order is not free.
  • The NNN conditions are one commuting family (Proposition 22.4, Proposition 22.5): Xa=−t(ξa)\mathcal X_a=-\transfer(\xi_a)Xa​=−t(ξa​) for the inhomogeneous Heisenberg chain (22.13), whose NNN sites are the particles and whose inhomogeneities are their own momenta ξj=kj/c\xi_j=k_j/cξj​=kj​/c. Lecture 18 solved it.
  • The nested Bethe equations (Theorem 22.7): (22.16) for the NNN momenta and (22.17) for the MMM spin rapidities, with E=∑kj2E=\sum k_j^{2}E=∑kj2​ — the spin rapidities carry none of the energy and act only as phase shifts. The quantum numbers have parities Ij∈Z+M2I_j\in\Z+\tfrac M2Ij​∈Z+2M​, Jα∈Z+N−M+12J_\alpha\in\Z+\tfrac{N-M+1}2Jα​∈Z+2N−M+1​, and a wrong parity is invisible in the logarithmic form. At N=2N=2N=2 they reduce to Lieb–Liniger in the singlet and to free fermions in the triplet (Example 22.8).
  • Hubbard (22.21): the Lieb–Wu equations (22.22)–(22.23) are the same system under k↦sin⁡kk\mapsto\sin kk↦sink, c↦U/2tc\mapsto U/2tc↦U/2t (22.24) — derived at N=2N=2N=2 in the tutorial and checked against exact diagonalisation at L=6L=6L=6, where 202020 of the 212121 singlet states are regular and the twenty-first is the η\etaη-pair; the general derivation is cited, and the regular solutions are not complete — at isolated couplings a colliding pair leaves a state that is neither regular nor a descendant (Theorem 22.9). On an even ring the model has SO(4)SO(4)SO(4) — with the η\etaη’s spectrum-generating for (22.21) itself and symmetries of H−U2N^H-\tfrac U2\hat NH−2U​N^ (Remark 22.10) — and an R-matrix that is not of difference form, which is why it sits outside Lecture 17’s machinery rather than inside it.
  • The hierarchy: for κ\kappaκ species the same R=u−iP\Rmat=u-\ii\permR=u−iP works, it is slκsl_\kappaslκ​-invariant, and the κ−1\kappa-1κ−1 levels of nesting are the nodes of Aκ−1A_{\kappa-1}Aκ−1​, coupled by the Cartan matrix (22.25) — with the self-term (b,β)=(a,α)(b,\beta)=(a,\alpha)(b,β)=(a,α) excluded, since Caa=2C_{aa}=2Caa​=2 would contribute a spurious −1-1−1, and with the source only at the node the particles attach to. For κ≥3\kappa\ge3κ≥3 the auxiliary monodromy has κ−1\kappa-1κ−1 creation operators, which is where the word nested comes from.
